title: The Evolution of Football Rules: Milestones That Shaped the Game
subtitle: From the first codification in 1863 to the digital era, discover how football rules have transformed the sport and what it means for Brazil
excerpt: From the 1863 meeting at Freemasons' Tavern to goal-line technology and VAR, learn how rules have changed football and its impact on Brazil.
author: Daniele Morais
contentHtml:
Since the first meeting in 1863, when English club representatives gathered at Freemasons' Tavern to define a set of rules, football has undergone transformations that accompany technical, social, and technological changes. Each adjustment to the rules reflects a dilemma – from sports justice to player safety – and has a direct impact on Brazilian fields, where the sport is a national passion.

The Roots of Codification: Freemasons' Tavern, 1863

The first Law of the Game, composed of 13 articles, established, among other items, the number of players (11 per team), field dimensions, and the prohibition of using hands, except for the goalkeeper. At the time, "offside" was defined in a rudimentary way, requiring at least three opposing players to be between the attacker and the goal line. This rule sought to avoid disordered "charges," but still left room for local interpretations.

International Consolidation: The Emergence of IFAB (1886)

In 1886, the four British federations – England, Scotland, Wales, and Ireland – formed the International Football Association Board (IFAB). The entity began to review the Rulebook annually, ensuring uniformity in competitions that, from 1904, began to expand to South America. Among the first modifications, the introduction of the penalty (1891) stands out, which transformed serious fouls near the area into scoring opportunities, bringing greater balance between attack and defense.

Major 20th-Century Changes: Penalties, Offside, Substitutions, and Cards

The last century was the stage for adjustments that redefined the game's dynamics. In 1925, the offside rule was changed to require only two opposing players between the attacker and the goal line, encouraging faster attacks and, consequently, higher-scoring matches. In the 1960s, FIFA authorized substitutions – initially one per game – allowing coaches to replace injured or tired players, a strategy that evolved into three substitutions, the standard in modern competitions.

The yellow and red cards, introduced at the 1970 World Cup in Mexico, brought a visual code that facilitated communication between the referee and players, reducing ambiguities in warnings. This tool became essential for maintaining discipline in high-tension matches, such as continental tournament finals.

Technological Revolution: Goal-Line Technology, VAR, and Their Implications

The 2010s marked the entry of digital technologies. The Goal-Line Technology (GLT), adopted in major tournaments from 2012, uses sensors or high-speed cameras to confirm whether the ball fully crossed the line, eliminating controversies that previously depended solely on human vision. Shortly after, the Video Assistant Referee (VAR) was implemented in the 2018 World Cup and major European leagues, allowing reviews of goals, penalties, direct red card decisions, and player identification. Although VAR has generated debates about the pace of the game, it has significantly reduced decisive errors, elevating the perception of justice.

Concrete Impacts on Brazilian Football

For Brazilian clubs and coaches, the evolution of rules imposes operational adjustments. The possibility of three substitutions, recently expanded to five in national competitions, requires squad planning that considers fatigue, tactical depth, and the tight schedule of regional and international tournaments. The mandatory adoption of VAR in the country's top divisions also pressures referees to adopt more rigorous protocols, reflecting on the credibility of decisions and the confidence of fans.

From a technical standpoint, changes to offside and foul marking rules influence the traditional Brazilian playing style – the so-called "samba" offense. With fewer opposing players between the attacker and the goal, coaches tend to explore shorter passing lines and rapid movement, while the discipline imposed by cards encourages a less violent and more strategic game.

Challenges and Future Perspectives

The future of rules seems to be heading towards even greater integration of data and artificial intelligence. Pilot projects using sensors in athletes' equipment promise to monitor effort intensity in real-time, potentially influencing decisions on substitutions and even generating new categories of fouls related to muscle overload. Meanwhile, discussions on standardizing safety rules – such as limiting studs on cleats – gain strength to protect players in increasingly physical confrontations.

Conclusion

From the modest list of 13 rules in 1863 to the sophisticated ecosystem of VAR and GLT, football rules have evolved in response to technical demands, the pursuit of sports justice, and technological advancements. Each change, although contested at the time, has contributed to making the sport more dynamic, safe, and globalized. For the Brazilian reader, understanding this trajectory is recognizing that football, beyond passion, is a living organism that renews itself with each generation, ensuring that the "ball" continues to roll in the country's and the world's stadiums.
